Lean Foundations
What Is Lean?
Deliver what the customer values, with less waste.
Lean is a way of working that delivers what the customer values using less time, effort, space and material. It does this by removing steps that add no value and making work flow.
Observe the process. Find the gap. Improve the standard.
Lean Foundations
What Is Value?
Value is what the customer is willing to pay for.
Value is defined by the customer: the right product, at the right quality and quantity, delivered at the right time and cost. Work that moves the product toward that need adds value.
Observe the process. Find the gap. Improve the standard.
Lean Foundations
Value-Added vs Non-Value-Added
Keep the value. Reduce the necessary. Remove the waste.

Value-added (VA) work changes the product in a way the customer wants and is done right the first time. Non-value-added (NVA) work uses time or resources without adding value. Some NVA is necessary today, such as required tests and safety checks: reduce it. The rest is pure waste: eliminate it.
Observe the process. Find the gap. Improve the standard.
Lean Foundations
The 5 Lean Principles
Five steps that turn customer value into a flowing process.
The 5 Lean principles are: specify value from the customer's view, map the value stream, make the work flow, let the customer pull, and pursue perfection through continuous improvement.
Value, stream, flow, pull, perfection: in that order.
Lean Foundations
Customer Value
The customer decides what is worth paying for.

Customer value is the benefit a customer receives from a product or service compared with what they give up for it: price, waiting and effort. Improvement starts by understanding that need in the customer's own words.
Ask the customer. Do not assume what they value.
Lean Foundations
Waste in Manufacturing
Anything that uses resources but adds no customer value.

Waste (muda) is any activity that consumes time, material, space, energy or effort without adding value the customer will pay for. Removing waste lets the same team deliver more value with less effort.
If it adds no value, question why it exists.
Lean Foundations
The 8 Wastes (DOWNTIME)
Remember DOWNTIME to spot the eight wastes.
The 8 wastes are Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-utilized talent, Transportation, Inventory, Motion and Extra-processing. The first letters spell DOWNTIME, an easy memory aid for waste walks.
Learn DOWNTIME, then go and find it.
Lean Foundations
Defects
Work that has to be fixed, redone or thrown away.

Defects are products or services that do not meet requirements and need rework, repair, re-inspection or scrap. Every defect consumes material, time and capacity twice and risks reaching the customer.
Prevent the defect at its source; do not just catch it.
Lean Foundations
Overproduction
Making more, or earlier, than the customer needs.

Overproduction means producing more than is needed, or before it is needed. It is often called the worst waste because it hides problems and creates other wastes: inventory, handling, space and risk of expiry.
Make what is needed, when it is needed.
Lean Foundations
Waiting
People, machines or material idle, waiting for the next step.
Waiting is any time when people, equipment or material are idle because the next step is not ready: waiting for material, approval, information, a machine or a test result.
Make waits visible, then remove their cause.
Lean Foundations
Non-Utilized Talent
Ideas, skills and experience that are never used.
Non-utilized talent is the waste of not using people's knowledge, skills and ideas. Operators often know the causes of problems best, but are not asked or not given time to improve.
The people doing the work hold the best ideas.
Lean Foundations
Transportation
Moving material more than the process needs.
Transportation waste is unnecessary movement of materials, products or information between locations. Every move adds time, cost and risk of damage without changing the product.
Shorten the route and reduce the moves.
Lean Foundations
Inventory
More material than the process needs right now.

Inventory waste is any raw material, work-in-progress or finished goods beyond what is needed for smooth flow. Excess stock ties up cash and space and hides problems such as unreliable machines or long changeovers.
Lower the water level to see the rocks.
Lean Foundations
Motion
Movement of people that adds no value.
Motion waste is unnecessary movement by people: walking, reaching, bending, searching or turning. It costs time and effort and can cause strain and injury.
Bring the work to the person, not the person to the work.
Lean Foundations
Extra-Processing
Doing more than the customer requires.
Extra-processing is any work beyond what the customer needs: extra steps, tighter-than-needed tolerances, duplicate checks or extra approvals and reports.
Match the process to the real requirement.
Introduction to Lean Six Sigma
What is Six Sigma?
Reduce variation so every output meets the requirement.
Six Sigma is a data-driven approach to improving processes by reducing variation and defects. It uses the DMAIC method and statistical tools to find and control the causes of variation.
Less variation means fewer defects.
Introduction to Lean Six Sigma
Lean vs Six Sigma Difference
Two approaches with different strengths.
Lean targets waste and lead time using tools like VSM, 5S and kanban. Six Sigma targets variation and defects using data and statistics through DMAIC. Choose by the type of problem.
Waste problem? Lean. Variation problem? Six Sigma.
Introduction to Lean Six Sigma
Why Combine Them?
Lean removes waste; Six Sigma removes variation. Together they do both.

Lean makes work flow by removing steps that add no value. Six Sigma makes each step reliable by reducing variation. Combined, they give processes that are both fast and right first time, which neither method achieves fully on its own.
Speed without quality is waste; quality without speed is cost.
Introduction to Lean Six Sigma
DPMO & Sigma Level Basics
Count defects per million chances to compare any process.

DPMO is defects divided by (units × opportunities per unit), multiplied by one million. It lets you compare simple and complex processes on one scale. A DPMO of about 3.4 corresponds to six sigma, while about 6,210 corresponds to four sigma.
Measure defects per opportunity, not just per unit.
Introduction to Lean Six Sigma
Common Misunderstandings & Why Leaders Need Lean Six Sigma
Lean Six Sigma is not headcount cutting, and it is not only for experts.

Common myths are that Lean means fewer people, that Six Sigma needs heavy statistics for every problem, and that it is a project for the quality department. Leaders need it because it gives a common language, facts for decisions and a way to build problem solvers at every level.
Leaders set the example; tools follow behaviour.
Introduction to Lean Six Sigma
Gemba: Go and See
Real answers are found where the work is done.

Gemba means the real place where value is created: the line, the store, the lab. Going to see means watching the process, asking open questions and checking facts before deciding. Reports describe a problem; the gemba shows it.
Go see, ask why, show respect.
Waste & Variation
Muda, Mura, Muri
Waste, unevenness and overburden are linked.

Muda is waste, Mura is unevenness in flow or workload, and Muri is overburden on people or machines. Uneven schedules create overburden, and overburden creates waste such as defects and breakdowns. Levelling the work often removes all three together.
Fix the unevenness and much of the waste goes with it.
Waste & Variation
Variation Concept
No two outputs are exactly the same.

Variation is the natural difference between outputs of the same process. Common-cause variation is built into the process; special-cause variation comes from a specific, unusual event and should be investigated.
Know which variation you are looking at before acting.
Waste & Variation
Types of Variation
Common cause is the system; special cause is an event.

Common cause variation is the normal, steady noise built into the process: material, method, machine and environment. Special cause variation comes from a specific event such as a wrong setting or a new supplier lot. Treat special causes one by one; reduce common causes by changing the system.
Do not react to noise; do act on signals.
Waste & Variation
Waste in a Real Plant: Example

In a filling and packing area, a waste walk often finds operators waiting for empty bottles, cartons carried long distances, rework of labels and extra stock at the line. Each finding is counted, photographed and given an owner. Fixing the top three usually frees hours of time every shift.
Count the waste you see, then fix the biggest first.
Waste & Variation
Mistakes in Identifying Waste & Waste Elimination Strategy
Waste is often hidden in "normal" work.

Typical mistakes are calling busy people productive, ignoring office and information waste, and looking only for defects. A good strategy is to walk the process, list waste by type, measure the biggest items, remove the cause rather than the symptom and then standardize the new way.
See it, measure it, remove the cause, standardize.
Waste & Variation
Lean Thinking vs Traditional Operations
Traditional pushes work through; Lean pulls value to the customer.

Traditional operations focus on keeping machines busy, large batches and inspection at the end. Lean thinking focuses on the customer, flow, small batches, quality at source and people solving problems every day. The shift is in mindset more than in tools.
Think flow and value, not just utilization.
DMAIC Overview
What is DMAIC?
Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control.

DMAIC is the five-phase Six Sigma method for improving an existing process: Define the problem, Measure the current performance, Analyze causes, Improve with tested solutions, and Control to sustain the gain.
Follow the phases; do not skip to solutions.
DMAIC Overview
Define Phase
Agree the problem, scope and goal first.
The Define phase clarifies the problem, the customer and their requirements, the project scope, the goal and the team. Key outputs are a project charter, a SIPOC and the voice of the customer.
A well-defined problem is half solved.
DMAIC Overview
Measure Phase
Understand current performance with reliable data.
The Measure phase establishes how the process performs today. The team defines measures, checks that the measurement system is reliable, collects baseline data and maps the process in detail.
Trust the measurement before you trust the data.
DMAIC Overview
Analyze Phase
Find and verify the causes that drive the problem.
The Analyze phase identifies possible causes, then uses data and tests to verify which ones actually drive the problem. Tools include fishbone, 5 Whys, Pareto, scatter plots and hypothesis tests.
Verify causes with data before improving.
DMAIC Overview
Improve & Control
Improve finds the fix; Control keeps it.

In the Improve phase the team generates solutions to verified root causes, tests them in a pilot and confirms the result with data. In the Control phase the new method is written into standards, monitored with charts and handed to the process owner.
A gain that is not controlled will slip back.
DMAIC Overview
Why DMAIC Fails & DMAIC Mindset
Projects fail from weak scope, weak data or weak follow-up.

DMAIC fails when the problem is too broad, data is skipped, the team jumps to solutions or no one owns the result after the project. The DMAIC mindset is disciplined curiosity: define clearly, measure before judging, prove causes and lock in gains.
Discipline in each phase beats speed through them.
DMAIC Overview
Six Sigma Roles & Belts
Clear roles make projects move.

The sponsor or champion owns the business need and removes obstacles. Black Belts lead complex projects and coach others; Green Belts lead projects in their own area part-time; Yellow Belts support with basic tools. The process owner keeps the gains after the project ends.
Every project needs a sponsor, a leader and an owner.
Define Phase Deep Dive
Problem Statement
Describe the problem with facts, not solutions.
A problem statement describes what is wrong, where, when and how much, compared with the standard or expectation. It does not include causes or solutions.
State the gap. Leave the solution for later.
Define Phase Deep Dive
Project Charter
The agreement that launches a project.
A project charter documents the business case, problem statement, goal, scope, team, timeline and sponsor. It aligns the team and management before work begins.
No charter, no shared direction.
Define Phase Deep Dive
SIPOC
Suppliers, Inputs, Process, Outputs, Customers.
SIPOC is a high-level map of a process that lists Suppliers, Inputs, the main Process steps, Outputs and Customers. It sets the project boundaries and shows who is involved.
Agree the boundaries before diving into details.
Define Phase Deep Dive
Voice of Customer (VOC)
What the customer says they need, in their words.

Voice of the Customer (VOC) is the collection of customer needs, expectations and complaints, gathered through interviews, surveys, complaints and feedback, and translated into measurable requirements.
Listen first, then translate into measures.
Define Phase Deep Dive
CTQ (Critical to Quality)
From a broad need to measurable requirements.
A CTQ (critical-to-quality) tree breaks a broad customer need into specific drivers and then into measurable requirements with targets or limits.
Every CTQ must be measurable.
Define Phase Deep Dive
Define Phase Mistakes & Strategic Project Selection
Choose the right project, then define it tightly.

Common Define mistakes are a scope too wide, a solution written into the problem statement and no baseline. Strategic selection links projects to business goals, chooses problems with measurable impact and keeps the number of active projects small enough to finish.
Pick fewer projects and finish them.
Define Phase Deep Dive
DMAIC Project Charter Example
A one-page charter for a DMAIC project.
A DMAIC project charter example shows the business case, problem statement, goal, scope, team and timeline on one page. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Agree it on one page before starting.
Measure Phase
Data Collection Plan
Plan what, how, when and who before collecting.
A data collection plan specifies what data to collect, the operational definitions, the sample size and frequency, who collects it, how it is recorded and how it will be used.
Plan the data before you collect it.
Measure Phase
Types of Data
Continuous data measures; attribute data counts.

Continuous data, such as weight, temperature or time, can take any value and shows small changes. Attribute data, such as pass/fail or defect counts, is easier to collect but needs larger samples. Choose the type before collecting, because it decides which charts and tests you can use.
Choose your data type before you collect.
Measure Phase
Check Sheet
Collect data simply, at the source.
A check sheet is a simple form for recording data as it happens, usually with tally marks by category, time or location. It makes patterns visible and data easy to summarize.
Easy to fill means more reliable data.
Measure Phase
Basic Statistics (Mean, Range)
The mean shows the centre; the range shows the spread.

The mean is the sum of values divided by their number. The range is the largest value minus the smallest. Together they give a quick picture of a process: for example, average fill weight and how far fills vary within a sample.
Always report centre and spread together.
Measure Phase
Measurement System Awareness
Is the measurement itself reliable?
A measurement system analysis (MSA) checks how much of the observed variation comes from the measurement system itself, through studies of repeatability, reproducibility, bias and stability.
Fix the gauge before blaming the process.
Measure Phase
Poor Data Collection Errors & Data Driven Culture
Bad data leads to bad decisions.

Common errors are unclear definitions, missing records filled in later, rounding and samples taken only when it is convenient. A data-driven culture makes data easy to record at source, checks it regularly and uses it openly in daily meetings.
Trust in decisions starts with trust in data.
Measure Phase
Operational Definition
Everyone measures the same thing the same way.
An operational definition describes exactly what to measure and how, including the method, the unit, the conditions and what counts as a defect, so that different people get the same result.
Define it so two people get the same answer.
Analyze Phase
Root Cause vs Symptom
Look past the symptom to what really caused it.
Root cause thinking means asking what condition allowed a problem to happen, and verifying it with evidence, instead of reacting only to the visible symptom.
Treat causes, not symptoms.
Analyze Phase
5 Why
Ask why until you reach a cause you can act on.
5 Whys is a simple method of asking 'why?' repeatedly, each answer based on facts, until a root cause is found that can be fixed. The number five is a guide, not a rule.
Each 'why' must be backed by evidence.
Analyze Phase
Fishbone Diagram
Organize possible causes before jumping to answers.

A fishbone (Ishikawa or cause-and-effect) diagram groups possible causes of a problem into categories such as Man, Machine, Method, Material, Measurement and Environment, so the team considers all angles.
List causes widely, then verify the few that matter.
Analyze Phase
Pareto Analysis
Focus on the vital few causes.

A Pareto analysis sorts categories from largest to smallest and adds a cumulative line. Usually a few categories create most of the problem. Start root cause work on the tallest bar, then redraw the chart after action to confirm it shrank.
Attack the biggest bar first.
Analyze Phase
Hypothesis Thinking
State a possible cause, then test it with data.

Hypothesis thinking turns opinions into testable statements, such as "fill weight varies more on night shift". Collect data to confirm or reject it before acting. This prevents teams from spending effort on causes that are not real.
Test the idea before you trust it.
Analyze Phase
Wrong Root Cause Trap & Analytical Leadership
The first cause found is rarely the root cause.

Teams fall into the trap of blaming people, stopping at the first "why" or choosing the cause that is easiest to fix. Analytical leaders ask for evidence, check that the cause explains the data and confirm by turning the cause on and off where possible.
Prove the cause before you fix it.
Analyze Phase
Cause-and-Effect Matrix & Affinity Diagram
Rank causes and group ideas before deciding.

A cause-and-effect matrix scores each input against its effect on the key outputs, so the team focuses on the inputs that matter most. An affinity diagram groups many brainstormed ideas into themes, making large lists easier to act on.
Sort and score before you choose.
Improve Phase
Brainstorming
Rules that bring out more and better ideas.
Good brainstorming sets clear rules: one topic, quantity before quality, no criticism during idea generation, build on others' ideas, and everyone gets a turn. Evaluation comes afterwards.
Generate first, judge later.
Improve Phase
Kaizen
Change for the better, a little every day.
Kaizen means continuous improvement through small, practical changes made by the people who do the work. Many small improvements, standardized and repeated, add up over time.
Small changes, made every day, by everyone.
Improve Phase
Poka Yoke
Make mistakes impossible, or instantly visible.
Poka-yoke (error-proofing) is a design feature or device that prevents a mistake from happening or makes it immediately obvious, so a defect is not produced or passed on.
Design the process so it is hard to get wrong.
Improve Phase
SMED Concept
Single-Minute Exchange of Die: faster changeovers.
SMED is a method for reducing changeover time by separating internal setup (done while stopped) from external setup (done while running), converting internal to external, and streamlining both.
Do as much as possible while the machine is still running.
Improve Phase
Pilot Implementation
Test on a small scale before full rollout.
A pilot run tests a solution under real conditions on a limited scale, such as one line or one shift, to confirm it works, find side effects and refine it before full implementation.
Small pilots prevent big mistakes.
Improve Phase
Improve Phase Risks & Sustainable Improvement Thinking
Test changes for side effects before full rollout.

Improvements can create new risks: new defects, safety hazards or extra workload elsewhere. Run a small pilot, check risks with a simple FMEA and involve operators. Sustainable improvement is simple, standardized and owned by the people who do the work.
A fix that people cannot sustain is not a fix.
Improve Phase
Solution Selection
Choose solutions with clear criteria.
Solution selection compares options against agreed criteria, such as effect on the root cause, cost, time, risk and ease of implementation, often using a simple weighted matrix.
Decide with criteria, not with opinions.
Control Phase
Control Plan
One document for how the process stays in control.
A control plan lists, for each key process step, what is measured, the specification, the method, the sample size and frequency, who checks it and the reaction plan if it goes out of limits.
Every check needs a reaction plan.
Control Phase
Control Chart
Separate normal variation from real signals.

A control chart plots data over time with a centre line and control limits calculated from the process itself. Points outside the limits or unusual patterns signal a special cause. Points within the limits show normal variation that should not be chased.
React to signals, not to every point.
Control Phase
SOP Standardization
A good SOP is the best known way, written simply.

Standard operating procedures describe the current best method, with key points and reasons. Use pictures, keep steps short and train people at the workplace. Update the SOP whenever an improvement is proven.
Standardize the best way, then improve it.
Control Phase
Visual Management
See the status of work without asking.
Visual management makes the status of work, standards and problems visible to everyone at the place of work, so teams can see at a glance whether they are on track.
Make it visible, then make it better.
Control Phase
OEE Monitoring
Track OEE daily to keep gains visible.
In the Control phase, OEE is monitored by shift on a simple board, with the top losses listed. Trends show whether improvements hold. A drop triggers a quick review and action before losses grow.
What is watched daily is kept.
Control Phase
Control Phase Failure & Building Continuous Improvement Culture
Without control, results drift back.

Control fails when standards are not updated, owners are not named or monitoring stops after the project. A continuous improvement culture builds daily reviews, audits and recognition so improvement becomes routine work.
Improvement is a habit, not a project.
Control Phase
Control Plan Example
An example control plan for one step.
A control plan example lists, for a key step, what is measured, the specification, method, frequency, owner and reaction plan. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Every control needs a reaction plan.
Advanced Statistics Basics
Mean, Median, Mode & Standard Deviation
Three centres and one spread.

The mean is the average, the median is the middle value and the mode is the most frequent value. Standard deviation measures the typical distance of values from the mean. A small standard deviation means a consistent process.
Know the centre and the spread.
Advanced Statistics Basics
Normal Distribution
The bell curve describes many process outputs.

In a normal distribution, about 68% of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. Many measurements, such as fill weight, follow this pattern when the process is stable.
Stable processes often form a bell curve.
Advanced Statistics Basics
Variation Interpretation
Read variation in context before acting.

Look at spread, shape and trend together. A wide spread suggests common cause variation; a sudden shift suggests a special cause; a slow drift may mean wear. Always compare the variation with the customer's specification.
Interpret before you react.
Advanced Statistics Basics
Statistics in a Real Plant: Example

A filling line records 30 bottle weights per shift. The mean is on target, but the standard deviation is high on one filling head. Fixing that head reduces spread, so the line can run closer to target and give away less product.
Stats point to where the problem lives.
Advanced Statistics Basics
Misreading Data & Data Driven Leadership
Averages can hide problems.

Common mistakes are using averages alone, mixing data from different machines and drawing conclusions from small samples. Data-driven leaders ask how data was collected, look at charts over time and base decisions on facts.
Ask how the number was made.
Advanced Statistics Basics
Run Chart & Stratification
See trends over time and split data to find patterns.

A run chart plots data in time order to show trends, shifts and cycles. Stratification splits data by machine, shift, product or supplier to reveal where problems come from. Used together, they quickly narrow the search.
Plot it over time, then split it.
Process Capability
Cp & Cpk Concept
Cp shows potential; Cpk shows actual performance.

Cp compares the specification width with six standard deviations of the process. Cpk also considers where the process mean sits, using the distance to the nearest limit. If Cp is good but Cpk is poor, the process needs centring.
Centre the process to turn Cp into Cpk.
Process Capability
USL/LSL
Specification limits come from the customer.

The upper specification limit (USL) and lower specification limit (LSL) define the acceptable range for a characteristic. They are different from control limits, which come from process data. A capable process stays well inside both specification limits.
Spec limits are the voice of the customer.
Process Capability
Sigma Level Link
A common scale for process performance.

Sigma level is a way to express how many standard deviations fit between the process mean and the nearest specification limit. A higher sigma level means fewer defects; it is a summary, not the goal itself.
Higher sigma, fewer defects, but keep the customer measure in view.
Process Capability
Process Capability Case Study

A fill weight process has Cp of 1.5 but Cpk of 0.8 because the mean runs high. Adjusting the set point centres the process, raising Cpk to about 1.4 and cutting overfill give-away. No new machine was needed.
Often centring is the cheapest fix.
Process Capability
Capability Misconceptions & Capability Strategy
Capability means nothing for an unstable process.

Common misconceptions are calculating Cpk on unstable data, using too few samples and ignoring measurement error. A capability strategy checks stability first, verifies the measurement system and reviews capability for critical characteristics regularly.
Stable first, capable second.
Process Capability
DPU, Yield & First Pass Yield
Count defects per unit and good output first time.

Defects per unit (DPU) is total defects divided by units. Yield is the share of good output. First pass yield counts only units that pass the first time without rework. A low first pass yield shows hidden rework.
Rework hides inside final yield.
OEE Deep Dive
OEE Formula
Put the three factors together.
OEE is calculated by multiplying availability, performance and quality. Each factor is a percentage of the ideal, so OEE shows overall effectiveness in one number.
Improve the factor with the biggest loss first.
OEE Deep Dive
Availability Loss
Was the machine running when it should be?
Availability is the share of planned production time that the equipment actually runs. It is reduced by downtime such as breakdowns, changeovers and waiting for material.
Every unplanned stop reduces availability.
OEE Deep Dive
Performance Loss
Did it run as fast as it should?
Performance compares actual output with what the equipment could produce at its ideal cycle time during run time. It is reduced by slow running and minor stops.
Small stops and slow speed hide here.
OEE Deep Dive
Quality Loss
How much of the output was good?
The quality rate in OEE is good units divided by total units produced. It is reduced by scrap, rework and start-up rejects.
Count rework as a loss, not as good output.
OEE Deep Dive
OEE Case
Use OEE losses to choose what to fix.
A packaging line OEE case breaks OEE into availability, performance and quality losses and targets the largest one first. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Fix the biggest loss first.
OEE Deep Dive
Fake OEE Trap & OEE Governance
A high OEE number can be false.
OEE is faked by shrinking planned time, using a slower ideal cycle or ignoring small stops. Good OEE governance fixes the definitions, audits data and uses OEE to find losses, not to judge people.
Honest OEE is more useful than high OEE.
OEE Deep Dive
Andon
A signal that calls for help immediately.
Andon is a visual and sometimes audible signal used to show that a process needs help, such as a light, a board or a cord. It allows problems to be raised and responded to fast.
Raise the problem fast; respond faster.
16 Losses
6 Big Losses
The losses that reduce equipment effectiveness.
The six big losses are breakdowns, setup and adjustments (availability losses), minor stops and reduced speed (performance losses), and start-up rejects and production rejects (quality losses).
Name the loss before trying to fix it.
16 Losses
Equipment Failures
Breakdowns are the largest availability loss in many plants.

Equipment failure losses are the time a machine cannot run because of a breakdown. Record each stop with time and cause, analyse repeats and act on root causes such as poor lubrication, loose parts or wrong operation.
Record every breakdown; fix the repeat ones.
16 Losses
Minor Stops, Startup & Speed Loss
Small stops and slow running add up.

Minor stops are short interruptions, such as jams or sensor faults, that are often not recorded. Startup losses occur before the process stabilizes, and speed losses occur when the line runs below its ideal rate. Together they can be larger than breakdowns.
Measure the small losses; they are rarely small.
16 Losses
Six Big Losses Case Study

A packing line records stops for two weeks. Minor stops on the capper cause 9% loss, more than all breakdowns. Fixing the bottle guide and sensor position removes most jams and raises OEE by several points.
Data reveals which loss is really biggest.
16 Losses
Hidden Losses & Loss Elimination Strategy
Some losses never appear in reports.

Hidden losses include waiting for material, quality checks, cleaning and operator shortages. A loss elimination strategy maps all losses from total time to good output, ranks them and assigns owners to the largest.
Map every minute from planned time to good output.
16 Losses
Condition Monitoring: Vibration & Thermography
Detect problems before they cause breakdowns.

Vibration analysis finds imbalance, misalignment and bearing wear in rotating equipment. Thermography uses infrared images to find hot spots in motors, panels and bearings. Both allow repairs to be planned before failure.
Listen and look before it fails.
SMED Advanced
Changeover Mapping
Map every step of a changeover.
Record the changeover on video, list each activity with its time and mark who does it. This map shows the real duration, waiting, searching and adjustments, and is the baseline for SMED.
You cannot reduce what you have not mapped.
SMED Advanced
Internal vs External
What must happen while stopped, and what need not.
Internal setup tasks can only be done while the machine is stopped, such as changing a nozzle. External setup tasks can be done while it is running, such as fetching parts, tools and documents.
Move every possible task outside the stop.
SMED Advanced
Parallel Activities & Quick Fixing Systems
Do steps in parallel and use quick fasteners.

Two people working in parallel can cut changeover time, as long as tasks are planned and safe. Quick fixing systems such as clamps, quarter-turn fasteners and locating pins replace bolts and reduce adjustment.
Fewer turns, fewer adjustments, faster change.
SMED Advanced
SMED Practical Example
Apply SMED to a real changeover.

A changeover reduction case films the current changeover, separates internal and external tasks, converts and streamlines them, then standardizes. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Film it, separate it, streamline it.
SMED Advanced
SMED Failure Reasons & Strategic Impact
SMED fails when it is not standardized.

SMED improvements are lost when there is no changeover standard, tools are not kept ready or training is skipped. Strategically, faster changeovers allow smaller batches, shorter lead times and more flexible response to customers.
Short changeovers make small batches possible.
SMED Advanced
Shadow Boards & Point-of-Use Storage for Changeover
Keep changeover tools and parts ready at the point of use.

Shadow boards show where each tool lives, so a missing tool is noticed at once. Point-of-use storage places tools, parts and materials next to where they are used, which removes searching and walking during changeovers.
A place for everything, next to where it is used.
Advanced VSM
Current State Analysis
Draw the stream as it really is today.
A current state map shows how the value stream works now, based on direct observation: process steps, data boxes, inventory, information flows and a timeline of lead time versus processing time.
Walk it and draw it as it is, not as it should be.
Advanced VSM
Lead Time Reduction
Lead time shrinks when waiting shrinks.
Most lead time is waiting between process steps, not working time. Reduce it by cutting batch sizes, inventory between steps and queues, and by linking steps with flow or pull.
Attack the waiting, not just the work.
Advanced VSM
Future State Design
Design how the stream should flow.

A future state map shows how the value stream should work after improvement, using Lean principles: produce to takt, create flow where possible, use pull where flow is not possible, and schedule at one point.
Design the future, then plan the steps to get there.
Advanced VSM
Flow vs Batch
Small batches flow faster than big ones.
In batch production, each item waits for the whole batch. In flow, items move one or a few at a time, so lead time, inventory and the risk of defects reaching many units all fall.
Make one, move one, wherever you can.
Advanced VSM
VSM Case Study
An illustrative value stream improvement.
A VSM case study shows the current state, the future state design and the actions taken. This example is illustrative; use your own measured data for real cases.
Current state, future state, action plan, review.
Advanced VSM
VSM Errors & Value Stream Strategy
A VSM without action is only a drawing.

Common VSM errors are mapping a value stream too wide, using guessed data and never implementing the future state. A value stream strategy turns the future state into a dated action plan with owners and regular reviews.
Map, plan, act, review.
Advanced VSM
Pull System: Kanban, Supermarket & FIFO Lane
Produce only what the next process takes.

In a pull system, Kanban cards or signals tell the previous process what to replace. A supermarket is a controlled store between processes, and a FIFO lane keeps a fixed, small queue moving in order. Together they limit inventory and keep flow.
Let actual use trigger production.
Line Balancing
Work Study
Study the method before timing it.
Work study combines method study, which improves how work is done, and work measurement, which sets the time it should take. Improve the method first, otherwise you are timing waste.
Fix the method, then measure the time.
Line Balancing
Time Study
Measure how long the work really takes.
A time study observes and times a task over several cycles, breaks it into elements, and records the repeatable time for each element, along with any irregular events.
Observe several cycles; record what really happens.
Line Balancing
Takt Time
The pace the customer demands.
Takt time is the rate at which products must be completed to meet customer demand. Takt time = available production time ÷ customer demand for that period.
Takt is set by demand, not by the machine.
Line Balancing
Bottleneck Removal
The step that limits the whole process.
A bottleneck is the process step with the lowest capacity relative to demand. It sets the output of the whole system; improving other steps does not increase output.
An hour lost at the bottleneck is an hour lost for the whole line.
Line Balancing
Line Balancing Case Study

A five-station packing line has one station at 52 seconds against a takt of 45 seconds. Moving one element to a station at 30 seconds and removing a walking step brings all stations under takt and raises output without extra people.
Balance the work to the takt.
Line Balancing
Line Imbalance Mistakes & Throughput Strategy
An unbalanced line runs at the speed of its slowest station.

Common mistakes are balancing on averages, ignoring variation and not updating the balance when demand changes. A throughput strategy finds the constraint, improves it first and balances the other stations around it.
Improve the constraint first.
Line Balancing
Yamazumi Chart & Work Combination Table
See the workload by station and person.

A Yamazumi chart stacks work elements for each station or operator against the takt time, showing overload and idle time at a glance. A work combination table shows manual, machine and walking time for one operator over a cycle.
Make the workload visible, then rebalance.
Inventory Optimization
Inventory Types
Three types of inventory along the stream.

Raw material is purchased input not yet used. Work in progress (WIP) is partly processed material. Finished goods (FG) are completed products ready for sale. Each type has different causes and controls.
Know which type of stock is growing, and why.
Inventory Optimization
EOQ Concept
Balance ordering cost against holding cost.

Economic order quantity (EOQ) is a classic model for the order size that minimizes the total of ordering and holding costs under steady demand: EOQ = √(2 × annual demand × cost per order ÷ holding cost per unit per year).
Use EOQ as a guide, then apply real constraints.
Inventory Optimization
Safety Stock
A buffer for uncertainty.
Safety stock is extra inventory held to protect against variation in demand and supply lead time. Its size depends on how much variation exists and the service level wanted.
Reduce variation to reduce safety stock.
Inventory Optimization
Inventory Turnover
Turnover shows how fast inventory moves.

Inventory turnover is annual cost of goods used divided by average inventory value. Higher turnover means less cash tied up and less risk of expiry. Track it by category, not only for the whole plant.
Stock that does not move costs money.
Inventory Optimization
Inventory Case Example
An illustrative case of excess stock.
An inventory waste case shows how excess stock built up, what it cost and how it was reduced. This example is illustrative; use your own data for real cases.
Cheap to buy can be expensive to hold.
Inventory Optimization
Overstocking Trap & Lean Inventory Strategy
Extra stock hides problems and ties up cash.

Overstocking happens through large minimum orders, fear of shortage and poor forecasts. A Lean inventory strategy sets limits by item, uses pull and Kanban for regular items and fixes the causes of uncertainty instead of buffering them.
Lower the water to see the rocks.
Inventory Optimization
ABC & XYZ Analysis
Classify items by value and by demand pattern.

ABC analysis ranks items by annual value: A items are few but high value, C items are many but low value. XYZ analysis ranks items by demand variability: X is steady, Z is irregular. Combining them sets the right control method for each item.
Different items deserve different controls.
Cost of Poor Quality
Prevention & Appraisal Cost
Spend on prevention to save on failure.

Prevention costs include training, process design and maintenance that stop defects from happening. Appraisal costs include inspection, testing and audits that find defects. Shifting money from appraisal to prevention usually lowers total quality cost.
Prevention is cheaper than detection.
Cost of Poor Quality
Internal & External Failure Cost
Failures cost most when they reach the customer.
Internal failure costs, such as scrap and rework, occur before delivery. External failure costs, such as complaints, returns and lost business, occur after delivery and are usually much larger.
Catch problems inside, prevent them at source.
Cost of Poor Quality
COPQ Case
Show what poor quality really costs.
A cost of poor quality case lists internal failure, external failure, appraisal and prevention costs for one product line. Illustrative case for learning; replace with your own measured data.
Make the hidden costs visible.
Cost of Poor Quality
Hidden Cost & Profit Improvement Strategy
Much quality cost never appears in accounts.
Hidden costs include extra inspection, expediting, overtime, lost capacity and damaged reputation. Profit improves when these are made visible, measured and attacked with problem solving.
Make the hidden cost visible.
Cost of Poor Quality
Defect Classification
Not all defects are equally serious.
Defect classification groups defects by severity, commonly critical (safety or legal risk), major (affects function or customer use) and minor (cosmetic). It guides sampling, reaction and priority.
Match the reaction to the severity.
TPM Integration
8 Pillars
The pillars that hold up TPM.

TPM is often described with pillars: autonomous maintenance, planned maintenance, focused improvement, quality maintenance, early equipment management, training, safety and environment, and TPM in offices, built on a 5S foundation.
Build on 5S, then raise the pillars.
TPM Integration
Autonomous Maintenance
Operators care for their own equipment.
Autonomous maintenance gives operators responsibility for basic equipment care: cleaning, inspection, lubrication, tightening and early detection of abnormalities, following clear standards.
Operators are the first line of equipment care.
TPM Integration
Planned Maintenance
Maintenance scheduled before failure.
Planned maintenance is maintenance work scheduled in advance, based on time, usage or condition, to prevent failures and keep equipment in good condition.
Plan the stop before the machine plans it for you.
TPM Integration
Breakdown Analysis
Run to failure, then repair.
Breakdown maintenance means repairing equipment after it fails. It can be acceptable for low-cost, non-critical items, but for critical equipment it causes unplanned downtime and risk.
Choose run-to-failure deliberately, not by default.
TPM Integration
TPM Case
An illustrative TPM journey on one filler.
A TPM case study shows how a team applied autonomous and planned maintenance to one machine. This example is illustrative; use measured results from your own site.
Start on one machine, prove it, then expand.
TPM Integration
TPM Misalignment & TPM Leadership
TPM fails when it is seen as a maintenance-only programme.

Misalignment shows when production and maintenance blame each other, or when TPM activities are not linked to OEE goals. TPM leadership sets clear targets, supports operator ownership and reviews progress at the gemba.
Equipment care is a shared job.
TPM Integration
Autonomous Maintenance Steps: Cleaning, Inspection & Lubrication
Operators clean, inspect and lubricate their own machines.

Autonomous maintenance starts with initial cleaning to find abnormalities, then sets inspection standards and lubrication routines that operators follow daily. Problems are tagged and fixed, and the machine is kept at its basic condition.
Cleaning is inspection.
8D Problem Solving
8D: D1–D4 (Team, Problem, Containment, Root Cause)
Form the team, define the problem and contain it.
D1 forms a cross-functional team. D2 describes the problem with facts. D3 puts containment actions in place to protect the customer. D4 finds and verifies the root cause and the escape point.
Protect the customer first, then find the cause.
8D Problem Solving
8D: D5–D8 (Corrective Action, Validation, Prevention, Closure)
Fix the cause and stop it coming back.
D5 chooses permanent corrective actions. D6 implements and validates them. D7 prevents recurrence by updating systems, standards and similar processes. D8 closes the report and recognizes the team.
Close the loop and share the learning.
8D Problem Solving
8D Case Study

A customer reports leaking bottles. The team contains stock, traces the cause to cap torque drift and a worn chuck, replaces the chuck, adds a torque check and applies the same check on other lines. Complaints stop.
Containment, cause, correction, prevention.
8D Problem Solving
Weak Root Cause & 8D Culture
A weak root cause brings the problem back.

Root causes such as "operator error" or "human mistake" do not explain why the system allowed the error. A strong 8D culture asks why until the system cause is found and treats every complaint as a chance to learn.
Blame the process, not the person.
8D Problem Solving
NCR & CAPA
Record nonconformance and act on its cause.

A nonconformance report (NCR) records what was wrong, where and how much. Corrective and preventive action (CAPA) removes the cause of the problem and prevents similar problems, with verification of effectiveness.
Record it, fix the cause, verify the fix.
Policy Deployment
Hoshin Kanri
Align everyone to a few breakthrough goals.
Hoshin Kanri is a strategy deployment method that selects a few breakthrough objectives, translates them into goals and actions at each level, and reviews progress regularly.
Few priorities, deployed to every level.
Policy Deployment
KPI Alignment & Cascade Goals
Every KPI should link to a company goal.

KPI alignment connects plant measures, such as OEE and right-first-time, to business goals like cost, delivery and quality. Cascading breaks top goals into targets for each department and team so everyone knows their part.
Everyone should see how their number links up.
Policy Deployment
Review System
Regular reviews keep plans on track.
A review system checks progress at fixed intervals: daily at team level, weekly at department level and monthly at plant level. Each review looks at results, gaps and actions, not just reports.
What gets reviewed gets done.
Policy Deployment
Policy Deployment Case

A plant sets a goal to cut complaints by half. It cascades targets to quality, production and stores, runs focused projects and reviews monthly. Complaints fall steadily because every team works on the same priority.
Focus everyone on a few goals.
Policy Deployment
Strategy Disconnect & Strategic Execution
Strategy fails when it is not turned into daily work.

A strategy disconnect happens when goals stay in presentations and teams work on unrelated priorities. Strategic execution assigns owners, sets milestones, provides resources and reviews progress regularly.
Strategy is only as good as its execution.
Policy Deployment
SQDCP & Leading vs Lagging Indicators
Measure safety, quality, delivery, cost and people.

SQDCP is a simple board structure for daily management. Lagging indicators, such as injuries and complaints, show past results. Leading indicators, such as near misses reported and audits done, show whether you are doing the things that drive results.
Track the drivers, not only the results.
Design of Experiments (DOE)
What Is DOE?
Change several factors at once and learn faster.

Design of Experiments (DOE) is a planned way to test how several input factors affect an output. Instead of changing one thing at a time, DOE changes factors together in a structured pattern, which shows main effects and interactions with fewer trials.
Plan the experiment before you run it.
Design of Experiments (DOE)
Factors & Levels
Choose what to change and by how much.

Factors are the inputs you change, such as temperature, mixing time or speed. Levels are the settings you test, for example low and high. Choose factors from process knowledge and levels wide enough to show an effect but safe to run.
Good factors and levels make a useful experiment.
Design of Experiments (DOE)
Full vs Fractional Design
Test every combination or a smart subset.

A full factorial design tests all combinations of factor levels and shows every effect. A fractional factorial tests a planned subset, which saves trials when there are many factors but mixes some effects together. Use fractional designs to screen, full designs to confirm.
Screen with fractions, confirm with full designs.
Design of Experiments (DOE)
Interaction Effect
Sometimes one factor's effect depends on another.

An interaction occurs when the effect of one factor changes with the level of another. For example, a longer mixing time may help only at a higher temperature. One-factor-at-a-time testing misses interactions; DOE finds them.
Factors can work together or against each other.
Design of Experiments (DOE)
DOE Case Study

A team tests mixing speed, time and temperature in eight trials to reduce viscosity variation. Results show temperature and its interaction with time matter most. New settings cut variation and are confirmed in production batches.
Few planned trials, clear answers.
Design of Experiments (DOE)
DOE Misinterpretation & Data Based Decision Leadership
Statistically significant does not always mean important.

DOE results are misread when trials are not randomized, noise is ignored or significant effects are too small to matter. Data-based leaders ask for confirmation runs and judge results by practical as well as statistical significance.
Confirm the result before you change the standard.
Design of Experiments (DOE)
Sampling Basics
Check a part to judge the whole.
Sampling means inspecting a selected portion of a lot to make a decision about the whole lot. Good sampling is random, representative and follows a defined plan for sample size and acceptance.
A sample is only useful if it is random and planned.
Risk Based Thinking
What is Risk?
Risk is the chance that something affects your objectives.
Risk combines how likely an event is and how serious its effect would be. Risk-based thinking means identifying what could go wrong, or right, before it happens and acting in proportion to the risk.
Think ahead, act in proportion.
Risk Based Thinking
FMEA Structure & RPN Calculation
Find and rank risks before they become failures.

Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) systematically lists possible failure modes, their effects and causes, rates severity, occurrence and detection, and prioritizes actions to reduce the highest risks.
Act on the highest risks before they occur.
Risk Based Thinking
Risk Mitigation Planning
Reduce high risks with clear actions and owners.
For each high risk, choose an action: avoid, reduce, transfer or accept. Give each action an owner and a date, then reassess the risk after the action to confirm it has fallen.
Every high risk needs an owner and a date.
Risk Based Thinking
Risk Case Example
An FMEA on a filling line ranks a missing seal as high severity. The team adds an automatic check and an alarm. Detection improves, the RPN falls sharply and the defect no longer reaches customers.
Rank the risk, then design it out.
Risk Based Thinking
Ignoring Preventive Actions & Proactive Leadership
Preventive action is cheaper than recovery.
Organisations often ignore preventive actions until a failure happens. Proactive leaders review risks regularly, fund prevention and reward people who raise risks early.
Reward the people who spot risks early.
Risk Based Thinking
Criticality Analysis
Focus effort on the equipment that matters most.
Criticality analysis ranks equipment by the impact of its failure on safety, quality, delivery and cost, and by how likely failure is, to decide maintenance priorities and strategies.
Not all equipment deserves the same strategy.
ISO 9001 Integration
Process Approach
Manage activities as connected processes.
The process approach in ISO 9001 defines each process with its inputs, outputs, owner, resources and measures, and shows how processes link. Managing the links prevents gaps between departments.
Manage the connections, not just the parts.
ISO 9001 Integration
Clause Structure
ISO 9001 follows a common high-level structure.

Clauses 4 to 10 cover context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation and improvement. This structure follows Plan-Do-Check-Act and is shared with other ISO standards, which makes integration easier.
The clauses follow PDCA.
ISO 9001 Integration
Risk & Opportunity
Plan for what could go wrong and what could go well.
ISO 9001 asks organisations to identify risks and opportunities that affect product quality and customer satisfaction, plan actions and check whether they worked.
Risks and opportunities both need action.
ISO 9001 Integration
Document Control
The right version, in the right place, at the right time.

Document control ensures documents are approved before use, reviewed and updated, clearly identified by version and available where needed. Obsolete documents must be removed or marked to prevent use.
Old documents cause new mistakes.
ISO 9001 Integration
Quality Audit Case

An internal audit finds that operators use an old SOP printout. The root cause is no control of printed copies. The plant introduces controlled copies with version numbers and a monthly check, closing the gap.
Audits find system gaps, not culprits.
ISO 9001 Integration
Compliance Only Mindset & Quality System Leadership
Certificates on the wall do not make quality.
A compliance-only mindset treats ISO as paperwork for the auditor. Quality system leadership uses the system to run the business: clear processes, real data and continual improvement.
Use the system to improve, not just to pass audits.
ISO 9001 Integration
Batch Traceability & Lot Control
Trace every batch from raw material to customer.

Batch traceability links each finished batch to the raw material lots, equipment, people and records used to make it. Lot control keeps lots identified and separated. In a complaint or recall, it shows exactly which product is affected.
If you cannot trace it, you cannot contain it.
ISO 14001 (Environmental)
Environmental Aspects
Identify how your activities affect the environment.

Environmental aspects are parts of your activities that interact with the environment, such as emissions, effluent, waste, energy use and spills. Each aspect can cause an impact on air, water, soil or people.
List the aspects before you judge the impacts.
ISO 14001 (Environmental)
Impact Evaluation
Rank environmental impacts by significance.
Evaluate each aspect by severity, likelihood, scale and legal requirements to decide which are significant. Significant aspects get objectives, controls and monitoring.
Focus effort on significant aspects.
ISO 14001 (Environmental)
Legal Compliance
Know and meet every environmental requirement.

Legal compliance means identifying applicable laws, consents and permits, such as effluent limits and hazardous waste rules, and checking compliance regularly. Keep evidence and act quickly on any gap.
Compliance is the minimum, not the goal.
ISO 14001 (Environmental)
Waste Management Strategy
Reduce, reuse, recycle, then dispose safely.

A waste management strategy follows the waste hierarchy: prevent waste first, then reuse, recycle and recover, and dispose safely only what remains. Segregate waste at source and track quantities by type.
The best waste is the waste never made.
ISO 14001 (Environmental)
Environmental Improvement Case
A plant measures solvent losses and finds leaks at transfer points. Closed transfer and better seals reduce losses and emissions, saving material cost as well as improving compliance.
Environmental waste is also money waste.
ISO 14001 (Environmental)
Reactive Environmental System & Sustainability Leadership
Do not wait for a complaint or a notice.
A reactive environmental system responds only after incidents or inspections. Sustainability leadership sets targets, monitors key aspects and builds environmental care into daily work.
Prevent, do not react.
ISO 14001 (Environmental)
Chemical Compatibility & SDS Essentials
Store chemicals safely and know their hazards.

Chemical compatibility means keeping substances that react dangerously, such as oxidizers and flammables, apart. The Safety Data Sheet (SDS) gives hazards, handling, storage, PPE and first aid for each chemical and must be available where it is used.
Read the SDS before you handle the chemical.
ISO 45001 (Safety)
Hazard Identification
Something that can harm, versus how likely and how bad.
A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm, such as a chemical, a moving part or a height. Risk combines how likely harm is to happen and how severe it would be.
Control the hazard to lower the risk.
ISO 45001 (Safety)
Risk Assessment Matrix
Identify, evaluate and control risks before work.
A risk assessment identifies hazards in a task, evaluates the risk, decides on controls, records the result and reviews it when the task or conditions change.
Assess before you act; review when things change.
ISO 45001 (Safety)
Control Hierarchy
Start with the most effective control.
The hierarchy of controls ranks risk controls from most to least effective: elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls and personal protective equipment (PPE).
PPE is the last line of defence, not the first.
ISO 45001 (Safety)
Incident Investigation
Learn from what happened to stop it happening again.
Incident investigation gathers facts about an event, establishes the sequence, identifies immediate and underlying causes, and agrees actions to prevent recurrence, without blaming individuals.
Investigate to learn, not to blame.
ISO 45001 (Safety)
Safety Improvement Case
A plant analyses near misses and finds many forklift and pedestrian conflicts. Marked walkways, mirrors and one-way routes are introduced. Near misses in the area fall and no injury occurs.
Near misses point to the next accident.
ISO 45001 (Safety)
Paper Safety System & Safety Driven Culture
How people think and act about safety when no one is watching.

Safety culture is the shared values, beliefs and behaviours about safety in an organization. A strong culture shows in open reporting, leaders who listen, and everyone feeling able to stop unsafe work.
Anyone can stop unsafe work, and is thanked for it.
ISO 45001 (Safety)
Permit to Work & LOTO
Control high-risk work before it starts.

A permit to work authorizes specific high-risk jobs, such as hot work or confined space entry, after hazards are checked and controls are in place. Lockout/tagout (LOTO) isolates energy sources and locks them so equipment cannot start during maintenance.
No permit, no work. No lock, no work.
Integrated Management System (IMS)
What is IMS?
One system for quality, environment and safety.
An Integrated Management System (IMS) combines standards such as ISO 9001, 14001 and 45001 into one system with shared processes, documents, audits and reviews.
One system, many standards.
Integrated Management System (IMS)
System Integration
Combine what is common, keep what is specific.
System integration merges common elements such as policy, document control, training, audits, management review and corrective action, while keeping specific controls for each standard.
Integrate the common elements first.
Integrated Management System (IMS)
Common Documentation
Fewer documents, clearer system.
Common documentation uses one manual, one procedure for shared processes and one set of records. This reduces duplication and makes the system easier to use and maintain.
Less paper, more clarity.
Integrated Management System (IMS)
Unified Audit Approach
Audit once, cover all standards.
A unified audit checks quality, environment and safety requirements of a process in one visit. It saves time for auditors and process owners and shows how the requirements interact.
One audit, one view of the process.
Integrated Management System (IMS)
IMS Case
A plant with three separate systems merges them into one IMS. Documents fall by about a third, audit days reduce and corrective actions are tracked in one register.
Integration saves effort and improves focus.
Integrated Management System (IMS)
Silo System Mistake & System Based Leadership
Separate systems create separate priorities.
Silo systems lead to conflicting procedures and duplicated work. System-based leadership looks at the whole organisation and makes decisions that balance quality, safety and environment.
Lead the whole system.
Integrated Management System (IMS)
Emergency Preparedness & Fire Safety
Be ready before an emergency happens.

Emergency preparedness covers identifying possible emergencies, planning responses, training people, providing equipment and holding drills. Fire safety includes preventing ignition, detecting fire early, keeping exits clear and using the right extinguisher.
Practice the drill before you need it.
Lean Culture Building
What is Lean Culture?
Shared habits of improvement and respect.
Lean culture is a workplace where people see problems as opportunities, follow and improve standards, go to the gemba, respect each other and improve every day as normal work.
Culture is what people do every day.
Lean Culture Building
Employee Involvement
People closest to the work know the problems best.
Employee involvement means operators take part in solving problems, suggesting ideas and improving standards. It grows through daily meetings, small team projects and quick response to ideas.
Ask the people who do the work.
Lean Culture Building
Kaizen System
A system that turns ideas into action.
A Kaizen system collects ideas, reviews them quickly, supports implementation and shares results. Simple tracking boards and regular recognition keep ideas flowing.
Make it easy to suggest and quick to act.
Lean Culture Building
Daily Review Mechanism
A fixed daily routine to review performance.
A daily review routine is a set sequence at a fixed time: review yesterday's results against targets, discuss today's risks, agree actions and owners, and check previous actions.
Same time, same place, same agenda.
Lean Culture Building
Lean Culture Case
A plant starts daily 10-minute team meetings and acts on at least one operator idea each week. Within months, idea numbers rise, small problems are solved locally and engagement improves.
Culture changes through daily habits.
Lean Culture Building
Resistance to Change & Culture Transformation Leadership
Resistance is information, not an enemy.
Resistance to change is a natural response when people feel uncertain, lose control or see risks. Listening to concerns, involving people and showing early results helps reduce it.
Listen to the resistance; it often points to a real risk.
Lean Culture Building
5S: Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain
Five steps to a clean, organized and safe workplace.

5S stands for Sort (remove what is not needed), Set in Order (a place for everything), Shine (clean and inspect), Standardize (make the best way the rule) and Sustain (keep the habit through audits and discipline).
5S is the foundation for every other improvement.
Change Management
Why Change Fails
Change fails when people do not see why.
Change often fails because of an unclear reason, lack of leadership support, poor communication and no quick wins. People resist what they do not understand.
Explain the why before the what.
Change Management
Change Model
Use a model to lead change step by step.
Change models such as Kotter's eight steps or ADKAR guide leaders through creating urgency, building a team, communicating a vision, removing barriers, creating quick wins and anchoring the change.
Follow a model; do not improvise change.
Change Management
Communication Plan
The right message, to the right people, at the right time.
A communication plan lists audiences, key messages, channels, timing and owners. It includes two-way communication so concerns are heard and answered.
Communicate early, often and both ways.
Change Management
Stakeholder Analysis
Know who is affected and who has influence.

Stakeholder analysis lists everyone affected by a change and maps their interest and influence. High-influence stakeholders are engaged early, and concerns are addressed before they become resistance.
Engage key people early.
Change Management
Change Management Case
A new shift pattern meets resistance. Leaders hold small group meetings, explain the reasons, adjust details from feedback and run a pilot. Acceptance grows and the change is adopted.
Listening reduces resistance.
Change Management
Emotional Resistance & Leading Change
Resistance is often fear of loss.
People resist change when they fear losing skill, status or security. Leading change means listening, involving people, supporting them with training and being consistent between words and actions.
Lead with empathy and consistency.
Change Management
Recognition for Kaizen
Recognize improvement to get more of it.
Recognition for kaizen acknowledges people's improvement ideas and efforts, publicly and promptly, which encourages continued participation. Recognition can be simple and does not need to be costly.
Recognize quickly, publicly and sincerely.
Digital Manufacturing
Industry 4.0
Connected machines, data and people.
Industry 4.0 uses sensors, connectivity, data analytics and automation to make manufacturing smarter. It works best on top of stable, standardized Lean processes.
Digitize a good process, not a bad one.
Digital Manufacturing
Digital OEE
Collect OEE data automatically and accurately.
Digital OEE uses machine signals to record run time, stops and counts automatically. It removes manual errors and shows losses in real time, but stop reasons still need operator input.
Automatic data, human understanding.
Digital Manufacturing
Data Automation
Let systems collect data so people can act.
Data automation captures data from machines, scales and systems without manual entry. It saves time, reduces errors and makes data available for daily decisions.
Automate collection, not thinking.
Digital Manufacturing
Dashboard System
Show the few numbers that matter, clearly.
A good dashboard shows key KPIs against target, trends and the top issues, updated regularly. It should be simple enough to read in seconds and lead to action.
A dashboard should trigger action.
Digital Manufacturing
Digital Manufacturing Case
A plant adds sensors to its filling machines. Real-time stop data shows that a feeder causes most short stops. A simple fix raises output, and the dashboard keeps the team informed.
Data makes the hidden visible.
Digital Manufacturing
Data Overload Trap & Smart Manufacturing Strategy
More data is not better decisions.
The data overload trap collects everything and uses little. A smart manufacturing strategy starts from business problems, chooses the data needed and builds skills to use it.
Start with the question, then the data.
Digital Manufacturing
Visual Factory & Status Boards
Make the status of the plant visible at a glance.
A visual factory uses signs, colours, floor markings and boards so anyone can see the standard and any abnormality. Status boards show plan versus actual, problems and actions for each area.
If it is not visible, it is not managed.
ESG & Sustainability
What is ESG?
Environment, social and governance performance.
ESG measures how a company manages its environmental impact, its responsibility to people and communities, and the quality of its governance. Investors and customers increasingly ask for ESG data.
ESG is business performance beyond profit.
ESG & Sustainability
Environmental Metrics
Measure energy, water, emissions and waste.
Environmental metrics include energy per unit, water per unit, greenhouse gas emissions and waste generated and recycled. Measuring them per unit of output shows real improvement.
Measure per unit to see real progress.
ESG & Sustainability
Social Responsibility
Care for people inside and outside the plant.
Social responsibility covers employee safety and wellbeing, fair practices, training and community engagement. In manufacturing, safety performance is often the first social indicator.
People first, always.
ESG & Sustainability
Governance
Clear rules, ethics and accountability.
Governance is how a company is directed and controlled: board oversight, ethics, transparency, risk management and compliance. Good governance builds trust with all stakeholders.
Trust is built on transparency.
ESG & Sustainability
ESG Improvement Case
A plant sets targets for energy and water per tonne, installs meters and runs Kaizen on utilities. Consumption per tonne falls and the data supports customer sustainability audits.
Lean tools improve ESG results too.
ESG & Sustainability
Greenwashing Mistake & Sustainable Leadership
Claims must match real performance.
Greenwashing means making environmental claims that are not supported by data. Sustainable leaders set honest targets, report real progress and invest in genuine improvement.
Report facts, not slogans.
ESG & Sustainability
Safety Observation & Behavior-Based Safety
Observe behaviour and coach for safety.

Safety observation means watching work, noting safe and unsafe acts and discussing them with the worker. Behaviour-based safety uses these observations to reinforce safe habits and remove the causes of unsafe acts.
Coach behaviour; fix conditions.
Business Excellence Models
What is Business Excellence?
Excellence is consistent performance across the whole business.

Business excellence means achieving outstanding results for customers, people, society and owners through strong leadership, processes and continual improvement. Excellence models give a framework to assess and improve.
Excellence is built, not declared.
Business Excellence Models
EFQM Overview
A European model for organisational excellence.

The EFQM Model looks at direction (purpose, strategy, culture), execution (stakeholder engagement, value creation, performance) and results. It helps organisations assess maturity and plan improvement.
Assess, then improve.
Business Excellence Models
Baldrige Concept
A framework based on criteria for performance excellence.
The Baldrige framework assesses leadership, strategy, customers, measurement, workforce, operations and results. It focuses on how processes are designed, deployed, learned from and integrated.
Strong processes create strong results.
Business Excellence Models
KPI Alignment
Link every KPI to the strategy.
In excellence models, KPIs are chosen to show progress on strategic goals, with clear targets, owners and review cycles. Too many KPIs dilute focus.
Fewer, linked KPIs.
Business Excellence Models
Business Excellence Case
A plant uses an excellence self-assessment to find gaps in leadership review and customer feedback. Two focused projects close the gaps, and the next assessment shows higher maturity.
Self-assessment shows where to start.
Business Excellence Models
Overcomplicated Systems & Enterprise Vision
Keep the system simple enough to use.
Overcomplicated systems create paperwork and confusion. An enterprise vision gives one clear direction so everyone understands priorities and how their work contributes.
Simple systems, clear vision.
Business Excellence Models
Lean Excellence Self-Assessment
See where you are today.
A Lean excellence self-assessment rates your area against key practices, such as 5S, standard work, visual management, problem solving, TPM and daily management, to find strengths and gaps.
Score honestly, with evidence, then pick two gaps.
Advanced Kaizen Strategy
Kaizen vs Innovation
Small steady steps versus big leaps.

Kaizen improves through many small, low-cost steps by everyone. Innovation makes larger jumps through new technology or investment. Organizations need both, and kaizen keeps gains from slipping between leaps.
Use innovation to leap; use kaizen to climb and hold.
Advanced Kaizen Strategy
Cross Functional Kaizen
Solve problems that cross department boundaries.
Cross-functional Kaizen brings people from production, maintenance, quality and stores together to solve problems no single department can fix alone, such as long changeovers or material delays.
Big problems need mixed teams.
Advanced Kaizen Strategy
Kaizen Funnel
Collect many ideas, select the best, implement fast.
A Kaizen funnel captures ideas widely, screens them for value and effort and moves the best into action. Tracking ideas through the funnel shows where they get stuck.
Many ideas in, the best ones out.
Advanced Kaizen Strategy
Impact Measurement
Measure the activity and the results of kaizen.
Kaizen metrics track both effort (such as ideas submitted, implemented and people involved) and outcomes (such as safety, quality, delivery and cost improvements linked to the changes).
Measure participation and results together.
Advanced Kaizen Strategy
Kaizen Case
An illustrative kaizen at a labelling station.
A kaizen case study shows the problem, the small changes tried and how the result was verified. This example is illustrative; replace it with measured results from your own site.
Show the before, the change and the verified after.
Advanced Kaizen Strategy
Idea Without Execution & Continuous Improvement Leadership
Ideas without action destroy trust.
When ideas are collected but not implemented, people stop suggesting. Continuous improvement leaders respond fast, support implementation and celebrate results.
Act on ideas quickly.
Advanced Kaizen Strategy
PDCA / PDSA Cycle
Plan, Do, Check, Act: the basic improvement cycle.
PDCA plans a change, tries it on a small scale, checks the results against the plan and acts by standardizing or adjusting. PDSA replaces Check with Study to stress learning from the results.
Small cycles, fast learning.
Financial Impact of Lean
Cost Structure
Know where the money goes.
Cost structure shows how total cost splits into materials, labour, energy, overheads and other costs, fixed and variable. Lean focuses improvement on the largest controllable costs.
Improve where the cost really is.
Financial Impact of Lean
Working Capital
Cash tied in stock and receivables cannot be used.
Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. Lean reduces it by lowering inventory and lead time, which frees cash for the business.
Less inventory means more cash.
Financial Impact of Lean
Productivity vs Profit
More output only helps if it is sold.
Productivity measures output per input. It turns into profit only when the extra output meets real demand or the freed resources reduce cost. Otherwise it creates inventory.
Link productivity to demand.
Financial Impact of Lean
ROI Calculation
Show the return on improvement.
Return on investment is net benefit divided by cost, usually per year. Count only verified savings, such as reduced scrap, overtime or material, and include all costs of the change.
Prove the money, not just the idea.
Financial Impact of Lean
Financial Impact Case
A scrap reduction project saves material and rework hours. Finance validates the savings, and the result is shown in the monthly cost report, building trust in the improvement programme.
Validated savings build credibility.
Financial Impact of Lean
Cost Cutting vs Lean & Business Thinking Leader
Cost cutting removes resources; Lean removes waste.
Cutting costs without removing waste often harms quality and morale. Business-thinking leaders use Lean to remove waste so costs fall while capability grows.
Remove waste, not capability.
Financial Impact of Lean
Verify Results
Prove the improvement with before/after facts.
Verifying results means comparing measured performance before and after a change, over a long enough period, to confirm the improvement is real and the problem has not moved elsewhere.
No data, no claim.
Benchmarking
Internal Benchmark
Compare lines, shifts and plants inside the company.
Internal benchmarking compares performance between similar areas, such as two filling lines. It is quick and the data is accessible, and best practices can be shared directly.
Learn from your best line first.
Benchmarking
External Benchmark
Learn from the best outside your company.
External benchmarking compares performance with other companies or industries. It shows what is possible and brings new ideas, but must compare like with like.
Look outside to see what is possible.
Benchmarking
KPI Comparison
Compare KPIs using the same definitions.
KPI comparison only works when definitions, units and periods are the same. For example, OEE must use the same planned time and ideal cycle definitions in every area compared.
Same definitions, fair comparison.
Benchmarking
Gap Analysis
Measure the distance to the target.
Gap analysis compares current performance with the target or benchmark and identifies the causes of the gap. It turns benchmarking into an action plan.
Know the gap, then close it.
Benchmarking
Benchmarking Case
Two lines making the same product have very different changeover times. The faster line's method is studied, standardized and applied to the slower line, cutting its changeover time.
Best practice travels inside the company.
Benchmarking
Copy Paste Mistake & Competitive Strategy
Adapt best practice; do not just copy it.
Copying another plant's solution without understanding its context often fails. A competitive strategy learns principles from benchmarks and adapts them to your own process and people.
Understand why it works before you copy.
Benchmarking
Horizontal Deployment (Yokoten)
Spread a good fix to every similar place.
Horizontal deployment (yokoten) shares a proven improvement with other lines, shifts or sites that have similar processes, so the same problem is prevented everywhere.
Fix it once, apply it everywhere it fits.
Supply Chain Optimization
Supply Chain Basics
The chain from supplier to customer.
A supply chain covers suppliers, inbound logistics, production, storage, distribution and customers. Its performance depends on material, information and cash flowing smoothly between links.
The chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
Supply Chain Optimization
Bullwhip Effect
Small changes at the customer, big swings upstream.
The bullwhip effect is the amplification of demand variability as orders move upstream in a supply chain, caused by batching, forecasting on orders rather than consumption, and delays.
Share real demand to calm the whip.
Supply Chain Optimization
Lead Time Reduction
Shorter supply lead time means less stock and faster response.
Reduce supply chain lead time by shortening order processing, working with nearer or more reliable suppliers, reducing batch sizes and sharing demand information.
Time is the hidden cost in the chain.
Supply Chain Optimization
Vendor Development
Help suppliers improve, and you improve.
Vendor development works with suppliers to improve quality, delivery and cost through audits, joint problem solving and shared targets.
Strong suppliers make strong plants.
Supply Chain Optimization
Supply Chain Case Study
An illustrative supply chain improvement.
